questions.stem: Which investigation predicts the visual outcome in branch retinal vein occlusion?
questions.explanation: In acute disease, the presence or absence of macular or foveal involvement determines the visual prognosis. Over the long term, permanent vision loss may be related to macular ischemia, cystoid macular edema, lipid residues or hard exudates in the fovea, and pigmentary macular disturbances. Ischemia is best detected using fluorescein angiography or OCT angiography.

questions.stem: What is the first-line management of CMV retinitis?
questions.explanation: High dose induction with IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg BID or foscarnet 90 mg/kg BID for 2 weeks, followed by low dose daily maintenance therapy. Oral valganciclovir 900 mg BID for 3 weeks, followed by daily maintenance therapy at 900 mg QD. Intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet are alternatives and useful for those who cannot tolerate intravenous treatment because of myelotoxicity, but they do not treat extraocular infection or the fellow eye, so combining with oral valganciclovir may alleviate this limitation.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with a headache for the last 2-3 weeks. Her uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination was normal with both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 18 mm Hg for each eye. Dilated fundus examination for the right eye revealed this picture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Background diabetic retinopathy with no macular edema

questions.explanation: Eales disease is a primary occlusive retinopathy of unknown cause. It usually presents in men aged 20-30 years, more commonly in those from India and the Middle East. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is characterised by bilateral idiopathic retinal perivasculitis with peripheral nonperfusion and neovascularization. A sea-fan of peripheral neovascularization may be seen. Vascular sheathing is seen in about 80% of patients, and both arteries and veins may be involved. All patients have confluent peripheral nonperfusion with a sharply demarcated border between perfused and non-perfused peripheral retina. Neovascularization is typically seen at this border and is most commonly found in the temporal quadrant. Vitreous haemorrhage is the most common reason for visual loss, and traction retinal detachments may develop. Treatment is with laser photocoagulation to areas of nonperfused retina. Eales disease has been associated with tuberculin hypersensitivity.
